name: Cuttack to Chandbali by canal
summary: Steamers left Cuttack and went down a canal to the port of Chandbali. Boats had carried salt and grain along the Mahanadi here for far longer than that.

source_refs.page: Imperial Gazetteer of India, vol. XI, pp. 92, 98
source_refs.note: p. 92: 'Steamers carrying passengers and goods ply three times a week from Cuttack city to Chandbali port by canal, and from Chandbali to Calcutta by sea.' p. 98: Cuttack is 'connected by canal with Chandbali and False Point'.

source_refs.page: O'Malley, Bengal District Gazetteers: Balasore (1907), pp. 10, 197
source_refs.note: p. 10: 'Chandbali, 20 miles from the mouth, is the most important port in Orissa.' p. 197: Chandbali stands on the left bank of the Baitarani, 20 miles from its mouth; land was leased to the India General Steam Navigation Company in 1877.

Cited for the cargo, not for the canal: 'formerly salt was an important article of export by way of the great road leading along the Mahanadi to Sembelpur and Berar ... more than three lacs of maunds being exported annually.'

caveats: The drawn line is a schematic, not a surveyed track: no source read here maps the canal, and the waypoints between the two ports were read off a modern map. Cuttack lies about 100 km from the open sea and ocean-going ships never reached it. Stirling and Hunter describe an older salt traffic that went inland by road and river boat to Sambalpur, not along this canal; they support the cargo only.
kid_line: Three times a week a steamer left Cuttack for Chandbali along a canal, then carried on to Calcutta by sea.

name: Chandbali to Calcutta by sea
summary: Steamers sailed from the river port of Chandbali up the coast to Calcutta. Odisha's own trade slowly drained away to that much bigger port.

source_refs.page: Imperial Gazetteer of India, vol. XI, p. 92
source_refs.note: 'Steamers carrying passengers and goods ply three times a week from Cuttack city to Chandbali port by canal, and from Chandbali to Calcutta by sea.' The chief imports of Cuttack district come from Calcutta.

source_refs.page: O'Malley, Bengal District Gazetteers: Balasore (1907), pp. 144-145
source_refs.note: 'The ports which trade with Chandbali and Balasore are Calcutta, the coast ports from Bombay on the west to Arakan on the east, and foreign ports, such as the Maldive islands, Ceylon, and occasionally Mauritius.'

caveats: The sea lane is a schematic drawn between the two ports; no chart or sailing direction was consulted. The two gazetteers are separate works but both are British official publications of the same decade, so they are not fully independent. Rice is listed because Stirling 1825, p. 194 records rice going from the small Odisha coast ports to Calcutta; neither gazetteer read here itemises this steamer's cargo.
kid_line: Three times a week a steamer left Chandbali for Calcutta.

name: Balasore to Calcutta
summary: A 19th-century report said Balasore was the only sea port Orissa could boast of at that time. Ships took rice and fine cloth north to Calcutta.

source_refs.page: O'Malley, Bengal District Gazetteers: Balasore (1907), p. 144
source_refs.note: 'At the commencement of the 19th century Balasore was the only port of which Orissa could boast.' Its trading partners are 'Calcutta, the coast ports from Bombay on the west to Arakan on the east, and foreign ports'. Trade was 'declining owing to the advent of the railway'.
'A considerable exportation of rice takes place from the several small ports along the coast to Calcutta.' 'Piece goods' heads the list of exports liable to duty.

Cited for the cargo: p. 40, the Orissa factors 'bought up at the lowest prices for ready money the fine muslins of Cattack'; p. 247, 'the Cattack and Balasor muslins formed an important item in the yearly Investments'.

caveats: Schematic line; no chart consulted. Hunter's muslin passages describe the 17th- and 18th-century English factories buying cloth at Balasore, not the 19th-century Calcutta run, so they support the cargo and not the route. Only the British period is listed, because the two sources that name Calcutta as the destination are both 19th century.
kid_line: Ships loaded rice at Balasore for Calcutta, and Balasore muslin went into the Company's yearly shipment home.

name: Gopalpur to Rangoon
summary: From the open beach at Gopalpur, steamers crossed the Bay of Bengal to Burma. Thousands of people sailed out each year to work, and most came home again.

source_refs.note: vol. XII pp. 329-330: Gopalpur, 'an open roadstead with no shelter whatever', a call for British India Steam Navigation coasting steamers; in 1903-4, 7,400 passengers went to and 8,300 returned from Burma. p. 152: Ganjam port exports go chiefly to Calcutta, Madras, Bombay, Rangoon and Moulmein.

source_refs.page: O'Malley, Bengal District Gazetteers: Balasore (1907), p. 144
source_refs.note: Chandbali and Balasore traded with 'the coast ports from Bombay on the west to Arakan on the east', which places the Burmese coast inside the same shipping circuit. Arakan, not Rangoon, is the port named.

caveats: Both statements about the Gopalpur to Rangoon link come from one work, the Imperial Gazetteer, so the tier stops at Probable. The Balasore gazetteer names Arakan and not Rangoon, and is cited only for the wider circuit. Neither source itemises a cargo, so goods is empty; the traffic they record is people. The open-water track is drawn schematically.
kid_line: In one year 7,400 people sailed from Gopalpur to Burma, and 8,300 came back the other way.

name: Manikapatna to Tamralipti
summary: A historian called Tamralipti, at the top of the bay, 'the first and foremost' of ancient Odisha's ports. The same patterned pottery lies at both ends of this coast, so boats seem to have worked between them.

source_refs.note: p. 118: 'people from different parts used to come by land and river route to the nearest port, then made a coastal voyage to different big ports, and thence made voyage to different foreign countries'. Tamralipti is 'the first and foremost' of the ports treated.

Rouletted ware from Sisupalagarh, Manikpatna and Radhanagara in Orissa is listed together with the same ware from Chandraketugarh and Tamluk in West Bengal, which the authors read as one Roman-period trade network.

'the land routes extended from Taxila to Kaveripattinam in the south and Tamluk in the east up to Broach in the west'; Tosali, Kalingapatnam, Tamralipti and Pithunda are named as the Kalinga centres 'which were all in the trade circuit'.

caveats: No source read here records a voyage between these two ports. The route is an inference from Patra's general model of short coastal hops and from rouletted ware found at both ends. Two of the three works share an author, so the independence is weaker than the count suggests. Tamralipti is in Bengal, at modern Tamluk; the claim that it was Odishan is a contested political one and is not adopted. Line schematic.
kid_line: Ships worked up the coast in short hops, from one big port to the next, until they reached Tamralipti.

name: Chilika coast to Sri Lanka
summary: Ships left the Chilika coast for Sri Lanka. A Chinese monk wrote that on a still night you could see a light shining over the island from here.

source_refs.note: p. 205, Charitra (Che-li-ta-lo) 'on the borders of the ocean ... Here it is merchants depart for distant countries'. p. 206: 'Going south 20,000 li or so is the country of Simhala (Seng-kia-lo). In the still night ... we see the surmounting precious stone of the tooth-stupa of Buddha.'

'The discovery of Shahasamalla's coin from Manikpatna in Odisha, Polonaruva in Sri Lanka and Kotchina in Indonesia testify to a maritime network linking coastal Odisha, Sri Lanka and Sumatra.' Manikpatna is Patra's preferred identification of Che-li-ta-lo.

p. 114: 'in ancient times prince Dantakumara and princess Hemamala had sailed to Ceylon with the Buddha's tooth relic from the port of Dantapura/Palur'. p. 112: excavation at Anuradhapura shows Indian cultural elements reaching Sri Lanka before Ashoka.
Rouletted Ware from Anuradhapura was analysed alongside the Sembiran and Arikamedu material, placing the Sri Lankan capital inside the same Bay of Bengal ceramic network as Kalinga's ports.

caveats: Anuradhapura is an inland capital, used here as the Sri Lankan anchor; the landfall would have been a north-western port such as Mantai, for which no Kalinga link was found. Xuanzang places Simhala south of Charitra and says a light was seen; he records no sailing. The tooth-relic voyage is a Dathavamsa tradition. Sahassamalla's coin is c. 1200 CE, the pottery some 1,100 years older. Two refs share an author. Line schematic.
kid_line: A Chinese monk wrote that on a still night you could see a jewel shining over the Buddha's tooth shrine in Sri Lanka.

name: Palur to Bali
summary: Palur was where ships stopped following the coast and turned into open sea for Southeast Asia. Indian pots of exactly the same kind lie buried at Sembiran in Bali.

source_refs.note: Palur was a departure port on the India-Southeast Asia route; the spread of rouletted ware suggests a trade link from the eastern coast to Southeast Asia.

Excavations at Sembiran in Tejakula District, north-east Bali, in 1987 and 1989 found Indian Rouletted Ware, a sherd of Arikamedu type 10 and a body sherd carrying a graffito identified as Kharoshthi, in deposits dated about AD 1-200.

Ptolemy's apheterion, a point of departure 'immediately to the south of Paloura (Palur), where ships bound for Khryse (the Malaya Peninsula) ceased to follow the littoral and entered the high seas'. Gerini placed it at Gopalpur; Patra prefers Mansurkota nearby.

Beal glosses Charitra as Chinese Fa-hing, 'city of departure', and equates it with 'Ptolemy's to apheterion ton eis ten Chrysen empleonton (lib. vii. c. 1, 15)' - the point where ships left the coast for the Golden Land.

p. 41: Baliyatra or 'Boita Bandana Yatra' at Cuttack marks the day Sadhaba mariners sailed for Bali, Java, Sumatra, Borneo and Ceylon on Kartika Purnima. p. 44, NOT p. 43 as cited before: Sembiran's rouletted ware is grouped with Sisupalgarh, Manikpatna and Tamluk.

caveats: Ardika and Bellwood say 'Indian', not Kalinga; the Odisha to Bali link is asserted by OHRJ p. 110 and by Nanda 2019, not by the excavators. Ptolemy's apheterion points to Khryse, the Malay Peninsula, not to Bali, and Ptolemy's own text was not read. Bali Jatra is a living memory, not a record, and dates nothing. Beal and Patra place the departure point differently, at Manikapatna and near Gopalpur. The 5,000 km line is schematic.
kid_line: Every year Odisha floats little paper boats to remember the sailors who set off for Bali on the Kartika full moon.

name: Chilika coast to Arikamedu
summary: Arikamedu near Pondicherry traded with the Roman world. Broken jars and the same patterned pottery turn up at Odisha's ports as well.

source_refs.note: p. 111: 'The rouletted wares of Manikpatna have much similarity with those of Sisupalagarh and Arikamedu.' p. 110: the same ware from Kaveripatnam, Uraiyur and Arikamedu is grouped with the Odishan finds as one Roman trade network along the east coast.
'the land routes extended from Taxila to Kaveripattinam in the south and Tamluk in the east up to Broach in the west'; Tosali, Kalingapatnam, Tamralipti and Pithunda were 'all in the trade circuit'.
'Arikamedu (11 deg 53' N; 79 deg 48' E), a well-known Indo-Roman trading station, is identified with "Pouduke" of the Periplus Maris Erythraei and Ptolemy.' Journal pagination not verified.

caveats: The tie is a shared pottery style, not a recorded voyage between these two places, so the tier stops at Probable. Amphora fragments are listed because they occur at Manikapatna and Palur inside the same Roman-period network; no source read here puts amphorae on this leg. Kaveripattinam belongs to the same network and would suit the line equally well. The sea lane is drawn schematically.
kid_line: The same rouletted pottery was found at Manikapatna and at Arikamedu, a thousand kilometres down the coast.

name: Manikapatna to Puri
summary: An English sailing book of 1679 gave the course from Manikapatna to Puri. Captains steered by the tall temple of Jagannath, which they could see far out at sea.

source_refs.note: Kempthorn (1679), folio 136-68: 'from Maneclapatam to Jauggernaut course is East-North East and distance is 10 miles.' The ship logs of Capt. Talbot (1680), Hide (1681) and Lake (1683) name Jaggernaut and Maneclapatam as landmarks for approaching the Odisha coast.

source_refs.page: O'Malley, Bengal District Gazetteers: Puri (1908), pp. 15, 196
source_refs.note: p. 15: 'The only port in the district is Puri, and this is nothing but an unprotected roadstead.' p. 196: 'The sea along the coast is fairly deep, and vessels can go close to the shore', but heavy surf blocks landing for most of the year.

caveats: Only Patnaik reports Kempthorn's direction, and 'Maneclapatam' is his reading of the name; the folio itself was not seen. His ten miles is far short of the roughly 45 km between the two places, so either the name or the figure is doubtful. The Puri gazetteer is cited for the coast, not for this leg. Patnaik's further conclusion that Puri worked as a port from the tenth century is his own and is not adopted here.
kid_line: A sailing book of 1679 told captains to steer east-north-east from Manikapatna to reach Jagannath.

name: Ganjam to Puri through Chilika
summary: Boats from Ganjam came north through a canal and across Chilika lake. They brought bamboo and carried away the spare rice of the southern villages.

source_refs.page: O'Malley, Bengal District Gazetteers: Puri (1908), p. 196
source_refs.note: Ganjam traders used the Ganjam canal and Chilika lake for boat traffic all year, bringing bamboo and taking away surplus rice.

p. 106: the Brahmanda Purana treats Chilika as a trade route, and Kushana coins at Gurubai on the strip between the lake and the sea 'suggests a trade route in the area'. p. 108: in 1810 pilgrims from the south came by road along the strip 'or in few cases by boats across the Chilika Lake'.

caveats: The gazetteer names 'Ganjam traders' and the Ganjam canal, not Gopalpur itself; Gopalpur stands in as the Ganjam anchor because the same gazetteer series calls it the district's chief port. The canal and lake line is schematic. Patnaik's Kushana coins and his Brahmanda Purana reference point to a much older Chilika route, but the boat traffic actually described is colonial, so only the British period is listed.
kid_line: Flat-bottomed patwa boats crossed Chilika all year round, bringing bamboo north and taking rice back south.

name: Jaugada to Palur
summary: Jaugada was a walled town up the Rushikulya river with Ashoka's orders carved on a rock. Scholars think its harbour was Palur, down at the river mouth.

source_refs.note: p. 113: 'The very location of the Asokan Edicts at Jaugarh, a place far away from the actual scene of the war i.e. Dhauli is an indication of its association with the port of Palur, a well known ancient port of Kalinga.' p. 109: Palur, near the Rushikulya, was a port of international repute.

'Ruined fort in Ganjam District, Madras, situated in 19 deg 31' N. and 84 deg 50' E., about 18 miles west of Ganjam town, on the north bank of the Rushikulya', carrying thirteen edicts of Ashoka on a granite mass.

Palur is placed 'just above the mouth of Rushikulya'. Przyluski derived Palura from Dravidian words meaning 'tooth city' and linked the name to elephant tusks, 'probably one of the important items of export'; Kongoda bred elephants of good quality.

caveats: No source read here describes a road between the two places. OHRJ p. 113 argues only that the position of the Ashokan edicts at Jaugada implies an association with the port of Palur, and that argument stands in one work. Ivory and elephants are listed because the Periplus and Xuanzang place both in this Ganjam and Chilika region, not because any source puts them on this road. The line follows the Rushikulya schematically.
kid_line: Palur may mean 'tooth city', and one scholar thought the tooth in the name was an elephant tusk waiting to be shipped.

name: The Orissa Trunk Road
summary: A great road was cut north from Puri through Cuttack to Balasore. Crowds of pilgrims walked it to see Jagannath, and carts carried paddy and salt.

source_refs.page: O'Malley, Bengal District Gazetteers: Balasore (1907), pp. 142, 146-147, 193
source_refs.note: p. 146: 'The principal road is the Orissa Trunk Road, which runs for a length of 95 miles from end to end of the district', linking Midnapore and Calcutta on the north 'with Cuttack, Puri and Ganjam on the south'; built by Captain Sackville 1812-1820. p. 193: 'also called the Jagannath road'.

Toynbee: 'The traffic from south to Cuttack passed along the eastern shore of the Chillika lake, between it and the sea, to Puri and thence followed exactly the line of the present great Jagannath road', and northwards from Puri through Cuttack and Jajpur to Bhadrak.

caveats: The road was sanctioned in 1811 and finished in 1825, so nothing earlier is claimed for this line. Ricketts wrote in 1841 that 'for eight months of the year it is in such a state that no merchants attempt to move goods by it' (Balasore gazetteer p. 143), and by 1907 its chief traffic was paddy and salt between Soro and Balasore only (p. 147). Patnaik's 'Van Den Brokes map ... 1960' must be a misprint and is not used. Line schematic.
kid_line: The road was built for pilgrims, and in 1827 a rich Bengali paid for rest-houses and bridges all along it.

name: Dhauli to Jaugada
summary: Ashoka had his officers carve the very same orders on rocks at Dhauli and at Jaugada. The two towns ran his new province of Kalinga together, so people must have travelled between them.

source_refs.page: Hultzsch, Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum I (1925), pp. xiii-xv, xxxvii-xxxviii
source_refs.note: Both sites carry the same two Separate Rock Edicts, addressed respectively to the Mahamatras of Tosali (Dhauli) and of Samapa (Jaugada); Hultzsch treats the two as the administrative centres of one Mauryan province, Kalinga.
Describes the edicts at Dhauli and Jaugada together, with the governor seated at Tosali - both sites presented as seats of one Mauryan provincial administration.

caveats: No source read here describes an actual road or a specific journey between the two sites; the connection drawn is administrative inference - both towns carried the same imperial edicts and belonged to one province governed from Tosali. The distance (about 100 km) and the line are schematic, read off a modern map, not a surveyed route. Do not raise this tier without a source describing real travel between them.
kid_line: Ashoka's officers had to visit both Dhauli and Jaugada, the two towns that ran his new province of Kalinga.

name: Udayagiri-Khandagiri to Pithunda
summary: King Kharavela's own carved message says he destroyed a market town called Pithunda. His army must have marched there from his capital, near the Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves.

source_refs.page: Jayaswal & Banerji, Epigraphia Indica XX (1929-30), line 11, translation p. 88
source_refs.note: 'And the market-town (?) Pithumda founded by the Ava King he ploughs down with a plough of asses' - Kharavela's own record of destroying Pithunda in his eleventh regnal year.

'The very location of the Asokan Edicts at Jaugarh, a place far away from the actual scene of the war i.e. Dhauli is an indication of its association with the port of Palur' - the authors read Kharavela's campaign as directed down this same southern coastal corridor towards Pithunda.
Pithunda 'could be located somewhere near Chicacole region of modern Andhra Pradesh', south of Palur along the same coast.

caveats: The inscription records the destruction of Pithunda, not the route the army took to reach it. Pithunda has never been excavated or located on the ground; the endpoint here is the same regional marker used in the pithunda port entry (centre of the Chicacole/Srikakulam region, read off a modern map), not a site position. Two of the three refs share an author (Benudhar Patra). The line is a schematic coastal corridor, not an attested march route.
kid_line: Kharavela's own rock-cut message boasts that he 'ploughed down' the market town of Pithunda with a plough pulled by donkeys.

name: Sisupalgarh to Manikapatna
summary: Sisupalgarh was a huge walled city a little way inland, and Manikapatna was a port on Chilika lake not far away. The very same kind of patterned pottery has been found in both places.

source_refs.note: Rouletted ware from Sisupalagarh, Manikpatna and Radhanagara in Orissa is listed together with the same ware from sites across the Bay of Bengal, read by the authors as evidence of one shared trade network.

'people from different parts used to come by land and river route to the nearest port, then made a coastal voyage to different big ports' - the general model of inland centres feeding the nearest port.

caveats: No source read here records a journey or road between the two places; the link is inferred from the shared pottery style and from Patra's general model of inland cities using the nearest port. Sisupalgarh lies roughly 70 km inland of Chilika by the shortest line; no bridging site or riverine link was checked. Line schematic.
kid_line: The same fine, dotted pottery has been dug up at big walled Sisupalgarh and at the little port of Manikapatna.

name: Palur to Sonapur
summary: Palur and Sonapur were both old ports on the south Odisha coast, a short sail apart. Ships likely worked their way down the coast from one to the next.

source_refs.note: p. 118 sets out the general model of short coastal hops between neighbouring ports. Palur (p. 121) and Sonapur (pp. 121-122, 'where river Bahuda enters into the Bay of Bengal ... 20 km away from Berhampur') are treated in sequence as ports of ancient Odisha along the same stretch of coast.

caveats: No voyage or record between these two named ports was found; the route is inferred from their proximity (about 55 km apart) and from Patra's general model of coastal hopping. Sonapur's own dating rests only on the paper's general framing of 'ports of ancient Odisha', not an excavation or inscription. Line schematic, drawn along the modern coast.
kid_line: Palur and Sonapur sit on the same short stretch of coast, close enough for a boat to hop between them in a day.

name: Sonapur to Barua
summary: Sonapur and Barua were both small ports further south along the same old coast. A Greek geographer wrote about places like these long ago.

source_refs.note: p. 118 sets out the general model of short coastal hops. Sonapur (pp. 121-122) and Barua ('Barua or Barwah ... from the accounts of Ptolemy ... one of the important trade centres', p. 123) are treated as neighbouring ports on the same ancient coast.

caveats: No voyage or record between these two specific ports was found; inferred from proximity (about 35 km) and Patra's general coastal-hop model. Both identifications ultimately rest on Maltby's 1918 Ganjam District Manual, not read directly in this session. Line schematic.
kid_line: Barua is named in a very old Greek book about India, alongside other little ports along this same coast.

name: Barua to Kalingapatnam
summary: Barua and Kalingapatnam both sat where small rivers meet the sea. Kalingapatnam was the bigger of the two, and its name means 'town of the Kalinga people'.

source_refs.note: p. 118 sets out the general model of short coastal hops. Barua ('now in Andhra Pradesh, 6 km from Sompeta', p. 123) and Kalingapatnam, at the Vamsadhara mouth, are discussed together as neighbouring ancient ports on the same stretch of coast.

caveats: No voyage or record between these two ports was found; inferred from proximity (about 75 km) and Patra's coastal-hop model. Line schematic, drawn along the modern coast.
kid_line: Kalingapatnam's own name means 'town of the Kalinga people' - a reminder of how far this coast carried the Kalinga name.

name: Dhamra to Chandbali
summary: Dhamra was the older port on this river mouth, made official in 1858. Chandbali grew up a little further inland and took over most of Dhamra's trade.

source_refs.note: The Dhamra estuary 'was declared a port by Government Notification, No. 877, of the 18th May 1858 ... As a port for native shippers, it ranks next to that of Balasor among the Orissa harbours.'

source_refs.page: O'Malley, Bengal District Gazetteers: Balasore (1907), p. 8
source_refs.note: 'The Dhamra ... is a fine estuary formed by the junction of the Brahmani and Baitarani rivers.' 'Chandbali ... absorbed the trade of the old port of Dhamra.'

caveats: Both quotations describe an administrative and commercial succession - Dhamra declared a port in 1858, then its trade drawn away by Chandbali, 20 miles further up the same estuary - not a description of boats plying between the two named points, so the drawn line and any specific cargo are schematic. Neither source gives a date for when the shift was complete.
kid_line: Dhamra used to be the busy port here, until the newer port of Chandbali, just up the river, took its trade away.

name: Cuttack to False Point by canal
summary: False Point was the spot where the Mahanadi river reached the open sea. A canal linked it to Cuttack, so goods could travel between the inland city and ocean-going ships.

source_refs.page: Imperial Gazetteer of India, vol. XI, pp. 92, 98
source_refs.note: p. 92: 'the chief trade centres are Cuttack city, False Point port, and Chandbali'; p. 98: Cuttack City is 'connected by canal with Chandbali and False Point.'

source_refs.page: O'Malley & Cousins, Bihar and Orissa District Gazetteers: Cuttack, 2nd edn (1933), pp. 7-8
source_refs.note: p. 7: 'False Point ... constitutes the only anchorage on the coast.' p. 8: a silting, exposed anchorage at the Mahanadi mouth - the sea end of the same canal system the Imperial Gazetteer names.

caveats: Neither gazetteer maps the canal itself; the drawn line is schematic, following the Mahanadi distributaries on a modern map. No cargo specific to this leg was found in the two sources read, so goods is left empty rather than copied from the parallel Cuttack-Chandbali canal entry. False Point's own entry describes a silting, exposed roadstead, not a sheltered harbour.
kid_line: A canal carried goods from inland Cuttack all the way out to the sea at False Point.

name: Balugaon to Puri across Chilika
summary: Balugaon was a fishing and grain town on the edge of Chilika lake. Boats and, later, trains carried its fish and grain on towards Puri and beyond.

source_refs.page: O'Malley & Mansfield, Bihar and Orissa District Gazetteers: Puri (1929), pp. 204-205, 212-213
source_refs.note: 'From Balugaon and Kalupara Ghat the greater part of the traffic is the export of fish and grain'; the District Fishery Officer's headquarters were 'shifted to Balugaon on the Chilka lake.'

caveats: Only one source was read, so the tier stops at Probable. The gazetteer documents Balugaon's fish and grain traffic and its later rail link, not a specific boat route to Puri; the line across Chilika and along the coastal strip is schematic, following the same lake-and-strip corridor as the existing Gopalpur-Puri-Chilika entry. No specific good in goods.json matches 'fish', and 'grain' is not tied to a named good in the source, so goods is left empty.
kid_line: Fishing boats at Balugaon brought in the day's catch, and grain from the villages went out the same way.

name: Manikapatna to Khalkatapatna
summary: Manikapatna and Khalkatapatna were both busy ports on the Odisha coast about 800 years ago. Chinese plates and coins have turned up at both places.

source_refs.note: Both sites are described with Chinese ceramics: Khalkatapatna's excavation (pp. 119-120) yielded Chinese celadon and porcelain with blue floral design, c. 12th-14th century CE; Manikapatna (p. 120) yielded rouletted ware, amphora and, in its later phase, Chinese wares.
Khalkatapatna excavation finds include 'Chinese Celadonware, Chinese porcelain'; Manikapatna's finds list (pp. 104-105) likewise includes Chinese celadon, porcelain and a Chinese coin.

caveats: The tie between the two ports is shared Chinese ceramic finds, not a documented voyage between them, so the tier stops at Probable (matching the precedent of the existing Manikapatna-Arikamedu entry). The two sites are about 50 km apart along the coast; the line is schematic, drawn along the modern shore. Khalkatapatna's Chinese material is dated c. 12th-14th century CE by most sources read, which fits the Eastern Ganga and early Gajapati era rather than the whole Somavamshi period; the somavamshi tag follows Khalkatapatna's own period list in sites.json.
kid_line: Diggers found the same kind of Chinese plates and coins at both Manikapatna and Khalkatapatna.

name: Pipli to Balasore
summary: Pipli was once the busiest port on the Orissa coast. When sand blocked its river, traders and English merchants moved their business down the coast to Balasore instead.

source_refs.note: p. 37: about 1514 the Portuguese founded a colony at 'Pippli, now a ruined and silt-locked village ... but then a fine harbour.' p. 40: silting of the Subarnarekha moved the Pippli factory to Balasore.

source_refs.page: O'Malley, Bengal District Gazetteers: Balasore (1907), pp. 9, 204
source_refs.note: p. 204: 'Pipli was once the most important port on the Orissa coast ... By the beginning of the 18th century the silting up of its mouth had ruined Pipli.' p. 9 ties this decline to Balasore's later rise as 'the only port of which Orissa could boast.'

caveats: Both sources describe a shift of trade from Pipli to Balasore as the Subarnarekha silted up, not a description of ships sailing this specific short hop, so the drawn line is schematic. The two sources give different dates for the Portuguese arrival at Pipli (Hunter: c. 1514; the Balasore gazetteer p. 204: 1599) and disagree on whether the English ever had a factory there at all (gazetteer p. 34 n., quoting Wilson's Early Annals) - see the caveats on the 'pipli' port entry itself.
kid_line: When sand blocked the river at Pipli, traders picked up and moved their business down the coast to Balasore.

name: Tamralipti to Mahatittha
summary: A 5th-century Buddhist book says ships often sailed between Tamralipti and Mahatittha, a great port in Sri Lanka. Both were busy stops for monks and merchants crossing the Bay of Bengal.

source_refs.note: The 5th-century Samantapasadika, Buddhaghosa's commentary, 'refers to ships often travelling between Tamralipti and Mahatittha.'

caveats: Only one source was read, so the tier stops at Probable; the claim is Dayalan's paraphrase of the Pali commentary via a secondary chain, not an independent reading of the Samantapasadika itself or of Buddhaghosa scholarship. No cargo is named. The sea lane is a schematic great-circle-ish line down the Bay of Bengal and across to north-western Sri Lanka, not a plotted sailing course.
kid_line: A 1,500-year-old Buddhist book says ships often sailed back and forth between Tamralipti and Sri Lanka's great port of Mahatittha.

name: Guangzhou to Palembang
summary: The Chinese monk Yijing sailed from the port of Guangzhou to Palembang on his way to study in India. He wrote down his own journey, stop by stop.

source_refs.note: 'Yi-Jing, who took the maritime route to India, left the Guang-Zhou region in China and visited Fo-che, Mo-lo-yu and Sumatra ...' Dayalan cites Chavannes's 1894 translation of Yijing's account.

caveats: Only one source was read, so the tier stops at Probable; this rests on Dayalan's paraphrase of Chavannes's 1894 French translation of Yijing, not an independent reading of a primary translation such as Takakusu 1896. No cargo is named - this was a monk's pilgrimage voyage. The sea lane is schematic.
kid_line: The monk Yijing wrote down his own voyage from Guangzhou to Palembang on his way to study in India.

name: Palembang to Kedah
summary: After Palembang, the monk Yijing's ship carried him on to Kedah on the Malay Peninsula. From there he waited for the winds to carry him further west.

source_refs.note: '... visited Fo-che, Mo-lo-yu and Sumatra ... proceeded northwest to Kie-tcha.' Dayalan cites Chavannes's 1894 translation of Yijing's account; Kie-tcha is read as Kedah.

caveats: Only one source was read, so the tier stops at Probable; this rests on Dayalan's paraphrase of Chavannes's 1894 translation, not an independent primary reading. Yijing's account also names stops at Mo-lo-yu and in Sumatra between Fo-che and Kie-tcha that are not modelled as separate ports here, so this line skips them. The sea lane is schematic.
kid_line: Yijing's ship called at Palembang, then sailed on to Kedah on the Malay Peninsula.

name: Kedah to Tamralipti
summary: From Kedah, Yijing's ship sailed past the Nicobar Islands and on to Tamralipti, the great port at the top of the Bay of Bengal. He later sailed the same route home again.

source_refs.note: 'Then, he proceeded east and reached the Nicobar Islands ... Proceeding northwest from these islands, Yi-Jing reached Tamralipti.' Returning to China 'he took the same route, landing again at Kie-tcha and Fo-che.' Dayalan cites Chavannes's 1894 translation of Yijing's account.

caveats: Only one source was read, so the tier stops at Probable; this rests on Dayalan's paraphrase of Chavannes's 1894 translation, not an independent primary reading. The Nicobar Islands are not modelled as a port here, so the waypoint there is schematic, read off a modern map. Yijing made the same voyage in reverse on his way home; this single entry stands for both directions.
kid_line: Yijing's ship sailed past the Nicobar Islands on its way to the great port of Tamralipti.

name: Cuttack to Sambalpur along the Mahanadi
summary: Boats went far up the Mahanadi river from the coast to Sambalpur. They carried salt, spices and pots inland, and came back loaded with diamonds, iron, silk and grain.

source_refs.note: 'Formerly salt was an important article of export by way of the great road leading along the Mahanadi to Sembelpur and Berar ... more than three lacs of maunds being exported annually.'

Mahanadi river towns 'carry salt, spices, cocoa-nuts, and brass utensils up to Sambalpur ... bringing thence, in exchange, cotton, wheat, oil-seeds, clarified butter, oil, molasses, iron, turmeric, tasar cloth, rice.'
Diamonds worked at Hirakud 'when Sambalpur was under native rule'; salt 'now brought by rail instead of river as formerly' - implying the river itself carried it before the railway.

caveats: Sambalpur is roughly 300 km inland; this corridor never reached the sea, and Cuttack stands in as the nearest major river hub, as in the 'sambalpur' port entry. All three sources describe actual two-way traffic (salt, spices, pots up; diamonds, iron, silk, grain down), not just two places that exist, so this sits above the inferred land routes elsewhere here. None gives a vessel type, a date, or a surveyed course; the line is schematic. Stirling's 'formerly' and the Gazetteer's 'now brought by rail instead of river' both suggest the river trade predated the railway.
kid_line: Boats went far up the Mahanadi to Sambalpur, swapping coastal salt for inland diamonds and silk.

name: Dhauli to Ujjayini
summary: Ashoka carved a rule at Dhauli that said an inspector must come all the way from Ujjayini, a city far to the west, every few years. This shows that officials really did travel this long road to check on Kalinga.

source_refs.page: Hultzsch, Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum I (1925), First Separate Rock Edict, clause AA, p. 97; identification pp. xxxvii-xxxviii
source_refs.note: 'But from Ujjayini also the prince (governor) will send out for the same purpose a person of the same description ... not (more than) three years.' The 'same purpose' is the inspection tour ordered earlier in the edict: every five years for the first tour, then at least every three.

'Then there were four large provinces governed by princes ... as governors or viceroys ... the viceroy of the west at Ujjain', alongside Tosali in Kalinga (east) - corroborating that Ujjayini and Kalinga were linked seats of one Mauryan administration.

caveats: The strongest evidence in this file for an inland route: the edict orders officials to travel this exact circuit on a schedule, not merely naming two related towns. Even so, no source describes the road itself - its course or stations - so the roughly 1,400 km line is schematic. The Dhauli copy is addressed to the Mahamatras of Tosali (see 'dhauli-separate-rock-edicts'); the identical clause appears on the Jaugada copy too, addressed to Samapa, hence the separate 'route-jaugada-ujjayini-road' entry.
kid_line: Ashoka's own rules said an inspector had to travel all the way from Ujjayini to Kalinga every few years.

name: Dhauli to Takshashila
summary: Ashoka carved a rule at Dhauli that said an inspector must also come from Takshashila, a city near today's Pakistan, every few years. That is one of the longest journeys named in any Kalinga inscription.

source_refs.page: Hultzsch, Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum I (1925), First Separate Rock Edict, clause BB, p. 97; identification pp. xxxvii-xxxviii
source_refs.note: 'In the same way (an officer will be deputed) from Takshasila also' - the same five-year first tour, then at least every three years, ordered for Ujjayini in clause AA.

'The viceroy of the northwest resided at Taxila', one of the four Mauryan provincial capitals alongside Ujjain (west) and Tosali in Kalinga (east) - independent corroboration of the administrative link.

caveats: As with the Ujjayini route, the edict orders an actual travel schedule rather than merely describing two related places, but no source maps the road itself; the roughly 2,600 km line here is schematic. This is the longest route in the whole atlas. The Dhauli copy is addressed to the Mahamatras of Tosali; the identical clause also appears on the Jaugada copy, addressed to Samapa, hence the separate 'route-jaugada-takshashila-road' entry. Cunningham's identification of Takshashila with Shahdheri, Rawalpindi district, is the standard one and is not independently checked here.
kid_line: An inspector had to travel all the way from Takshashila, near modern Pakistan, to check on Kalinga.

name: Jaugada to Ujjayini
summary: The same rule Ashoka carved at Dhauli was carved again at Jaugada: an inspector had to come from Ujjayini every few years. Jaugada and Dhauli were the two towns that ran Ashoka's new province of Kalinga.

source_refs.page: Hultzsch, Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum I (1925), First Separate Rock Edict, clause AA, p. 97 (Jaugada copy pp. 111-116); identification pp. xxxvii-xxxviii
source_refs.note: 'But from Ujjayini also the prince (governor) will send out for the same purpose a person of the same description ... not (more than) three years.' This clause is part of the same edict inscribed at both Dhauli and Jaugada; the Jaugada copy is addressed to the Mahamatras of Samapa.
'Then there were four large provinces governed by princes ... the viceroy of the west at Ujjain', alongside Tosali in Kalinga (east) - independent corroboration of the administrative link.

caveats: As with the Dhauli entry, the edict orders a real travel schedule, but no source maps the road itself; the line is schematic. Jaugada's copy of this edict is addressed to Samapa's officials, not Tosali's, so this is recorded as a separate route from 'route-dhauli-ujjayini-road' rather than a duplicate, even though both rest on the same underlying clause of the edict.
kid_line: The same rule was carved again at Jaugada: an officer had to travel there from Ujjayini every few years.

name: Jaugada to Takshashila
summary: The same rule Ashoka carved at Dhauli was carved again at Jaugada: an inspector had to come from Takshashila, near today's Pakistan, every few years. It shows how far Ashoka's officials journeyed to check on Kalinga.

source_refs.page: Hultzsch, Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum I (1925), First Separate Rock Edict, clause BB, p. 97 (Jaugada copy pp. 111-116); identification pp. xxxvii-xxxviii
source_refs.note: 'In the same way (an officer will be deputed) from Takshasila also.' This clause is part of the same edict inscribed at both Dhauli and Jaugada; the Jaugada copy is addressed to the Mahamatras of Samapa.

'The viceroy of the northwest resided at Taxila', one of the four Mauryan provincial capitals alongside Ujjain (west) and Tosali in Kalinga (east) - independent corroboration of the administrative link.

caveats: As with the other three edict-based routes, the inscription orders a real travel schedule rather than merely naming two related places, but no source maps the road itself; the line is schematic. Jaugada's copy of this edict is addressed to Samapa's officials, not Tosali's, so this is kept as a separate route from 'route-dhauli-takshashila-road'. This is the longest land route in the atlas after its Dhauli counterpart.
kid_line: The same rule was carved again at Jaugada: an officer had to travel from Takshashila, near modern Pakistan, to check on Kalinga.
